lessons.text: Bid validity shorter than the evaluation and approval period forced re-bidding on two works packages.
Splitting a large works contract into lots raised the number of bidders.
Late land acquisition delayed site handover.
Prequalifying bidders for the complex bridge package shortened evaluation.
Late approval of time amendments left contractors without cover.
A single consultant framework weakened independent review of design changes.

Mock supervision report 1. Cumulative disbursement is 2 percent of the loan. Mobilisation of the first works contract is under way.
Mock supervision report 2. Progress toward the development objective remains Satisfactory. Overall risk is Moderate. Contract REF-001 is behind its mobilisation schedule.
Mock supervision report 2. Cumulative disbursement is 6 percent of the loan. Land acquisition delays are noted.
Mock supervision report 3. Progress toward the development objective is downgraded from Satisfactory to Moderately Unsatisfactory. Overall risk rises from Moderate to Substantial.
Mock supervision report 3. Fiduciary risk is Substantial: procurement packages were re-bid after low participation, and bid validity expired on two packages.
Mock completion report. Bid validity shorter than the evaluation and approval period forced re-bidding on two works packages and added months to the closing date.
Mock completion report. Splitting a large works contract into smaller lots raised the number of bidders and shortened the time to award.
Mock completion report. Late land acquisition delayed site handover; contract amendments extended time by 14 months in total.
Mock procurement guidance. Bid validity should cover the evaluation period plus the time for approvals and contract signing, with a margin.
Mock procurement guidance. Performance security for works contracts is commonly set between five and ten percent of the contract price.
Mock procurement guidance. Evaluation of bids is normally completed within a few weeks of bid opening for works contracts without a prequalification stage.
Mock supervision report for P-MOCK-002. Progress toward the development objective is rated Satisfactory and overall risk is Moderate.
Mock supervision report for P-MOCK-002. The pipe supply tender was cancelled when no compliant bids were received and was re-issued.
Mock supervision report 2 for P-MOCK-002. Ratings are unchanged. Disbursement is 9 percent of the loan.
Mock supervision report for P-MOCK-003. The project is not yet effective; progress toward the objective is rated Satisfactory.
Mock completion report. Prequalifying bidders for the complex bridge package reduced the number of unresponsive bids and shortened evaluation by about three weeks.
Mock completion report. Contract amendments for time were approved late, so liquidated damages could not be applied and two contractors stayed on site without cover.
Mock completion report. A single consultant framework for design and supervision reduced procurement time but weakened independent review of design changes.
Mock procurement guidance. The evaluation report should record each bidder against the stated criteria, and the award should be made within the bid validity period.
Mock procurement guidance. A standstill period lets unsuccessful bidders ask for a debrief before the contract is signed.
Mock procurement guidance. Amendments that change time or value should be recorded with a reason, approved before they take effect and reported with the next supervision report.
Mock procurement guidance. Planned and actual dates for mobilisation and completion should be recorded for every works contract so delays can be seen early.
Mock procurement guidance. Quality-based selection suits assignments where the quality of the advice matters more than cost; the shortlist normally has between three and six firms.
Mock appraisal document for P-MOCK-001. Works above the national threshold are procured by open competitive tender; REF-001 and REF-002 are the first two packages.
Mock appraisal document for P-MOCK-001. Land acquisition and late payment to contractors are identified as the main implementation risks.
Mock procurement plan for P-MOCK-001. Contracts REF-003 and REF-004 are shopping and limited competitive packages with expected signing in the first half of 2026.
Mock procurement plan for P-MOCK-001. Contract REF-005 covers survey services selected on quality, and REF-006 covers drainage works.
Mock bid evaluation report for contract REF-001. Three bids were received and opened; the lowest evaluated bid was recommended for award.
Mock safeguards plan for P-MOCK-001. Contractors prepare a site-specific management plan before mobilisation; contract REF-002 requires river protection measures.

The World Bank Implementation Status & Results Report Vietnam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) Vietnam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) EAST ASIA AND PACIFIC | Vietnam | Transport Global Practice | IBRD/IDA | Investment Project Financing | FY 2014 | Seq No: 17 | ARCHIVED on 11-Sep-2022 | ISR52319 | Implementing Agencies: Project Management Unit No. 3 (PMU3), The Socialist Republic of Vietnam Key Dates Key Project Dates Bank Approval Date: 12-Dec-2013 Effectiveness Date: 14-Jan-2014 Planned Mid Term Review Date: 09-Jan-2017 Actual Mid-Term Review Date: 09-Jan-2017 Original Closing Date: 31-Dec-2020 Revised Closing Date: 31-Dec-2022 pdoTable Project Development Objectives Project Development Objective (from Project Appraisal Document) The proposed Project Development Objective (PDO) is to improve the efficiency and sustainability of the national road asset management and maintenance practices performed by the Ministry of Transport on national roads in Vietnam.

Has the Project Development Objective been changed since Board Approval of the Project Objective? No Components Table Name Component A: Road Asset Management System (RAMS) Development:(Cost $10.00 M) Component B: Road Asset Preservation:(Cost $156.60 M) Component C: Road Asset Improvement:(Cost $133.40 M) Component D: Institutional Strengthening Program:(Cost $1.70 M) Overall Ratings Name Previous Rating Current Rating Progress towards achievement of PDO Satisfactory Satisfactory Overall Implementation Progress (IP) Satisfactory Moderately Satisfactory Overall Risk Rating Low Low Implementation Status and Key Decisions The project was approved by the Board on December 12, 2013 with the Financing Agreement signed on January 14, 2014 and became effective on April 11, 2014. Overall, the project implementation has progressed well with satisfactory completion of all components as originally planned. All PDO and intermediate indicators have fully achieved or overachieved their targets. For the original scope, contracts for goods, works and services have been completed successfully. The Road Asset Management System (RAMS) has been developed and is fully operational to effectively enhance the preparation of the medium term investment plan (MTIP) for 2021-2025 as well as prioritization of the maintenance plan for the whole national highway network in a sustainable and transparent approach. The institutional strengthening program was satisfactorily completed, too.

The implementation of the first additional activities (using US$31.98 million) for improvement of NH6 in Son La and NH2 in Ha Giang. All seven civil works contracts have been progressing very well and are on track for completion by the current project closing date of December 31, 9/11/2022 Page 1 of 7 The World Bank Implementation Status & Results Report Vietnam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) 2022. Land acquisition and resettlement (LAR) activities which started in early 2020 have reached 98 percentage completion for NH6 and 99 percentage completion for NH2. Implementation of the second additional activity for NH9 improvement (using US$21.64 million) has been seriously delayed. The consultants for construction supervision, safeguards monitoring and financial audit have been mobilized since March 2022. Two civil works contracts of about US$9 million were signed in March and construction has started from March 31, 2022. However, the LAR activities which are funded/implemented by Quang Tri province have been seriously delayed. So far, only 4.5 km of land from either side of the road have been cleared. The main cause of this delay is the low estimates for the total LAR costs of VND 75 billions evaluated in 2020 compared to the current market cost of VND 345 billion. The Provincial People’s Committee (PPC) is only able to allocate VND75 billion for LAR activities by July 2022. The remaining VND 270 billion has been recently secured in August 2022.

However, it is very unlikely that the LAR activities could be completed and handed over by September 2022 to allow adequate time for works to be constructed with acceptable quality. This is putting in jeopardy the implementation of the NH9 improvement. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL Context 1. At the time of project appraisal, Viet Nam was enjoying a period of rapid economic growth and livelihoods had improved greatly. Real gross domestic product (GDP) had increased at an average annual rate of 7.4 percent between 1990 and 2010, placing the country among the top five globally for growth over that period. In fact, between 1993 and 2014, Viet Nam's amazing rise from a low-income to middle-income position pulled 40 million people out of poverty; in other words, the proportion of people living in poverty fell from 60 percent in 1993 to 14 percent in 2014.1 Nevertheless, rural households with limited access to economic development and opportunities remained at risk of extreme poverty, and they were the targeted beneficiaries of this project. 2. Viet Nam's development trajectory was significantly influenced by infrastructure investment.

Annual infrastructure spending was maintained at between nine and 10 percent of GDP, with transport accounting for nearly half of this amount over the same period (1990 to 2010). As urbanization continued to spread (it was anticipated that by 2020, about 50 percent of the Vietnamese population would live in urban areas), further expansion of the road, rail, and inland waterway transport networks was necessary to relieve bottlenecks, improve productivity, and meet important growth and poverty reduction targets. Sectoral context 3. Viet Nam’s road transport network has improved over the past decades. At appraisal, the overall length of the entire road network in Viet Nam was approximately 210,000 km, of which 17,199 km were national highways, and 17,450 km were provincial roads. The bulk of the 131,951 km (about 63 percent) comprised rural roads. The density of the road network was 677 km per 1,000 km2 and 2.41 km per 1,000 people. Although the network had grown, 30 percent of Viet Nam's national highways were still in "poor" or "very poor" condition. Overall, only roughly half of the road network was paved. 4. The Government of Viet Nam (GoV) invested in transport infrastructure. It recognized that to address sectoral challenges and maintain current road conditions, the allocation of financing to strengthen infrastructure would be crucial.

Analysis in 2012 showed that preservation of the existing state of the country’s roads (routine/periodic maintenance and rehabilitation) would cost US$ 360 million per year. The government adopted a strategy to increase recurrent expenditure on road maintenance. Through the creation of a Road Maintenance Fund (RMF), the GoV expected to increase revenue streams for road maintenance, and therefore asked the World Bank for assistance to finance upgrading of the Road Asset Management System (RAMS) to improve planning of regular maintenance and upgrading of strategically chosen corridors of the National Highway (NH) network. 6. The Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (VRAMP) was designed to contribute cutting-edge thinking on planning and prioritization of road maintenance for sustainability. VRAMP is based on the World Bank’s engagement with the GoV and lessons learned from Road Network Improvement Project (RNIP) P059663 (US$ 225.26 million) which supported an efficient transport network and preservation of existing assets.

VRAMP supported the Bank’s Country Partnership Strategy (CPS) FY12–FY16 Pillar 1: strengthening Viet Nam's competitiveness in the regional and global economy through improved quality and efficiency of infrastructure services aimed at reduced travel times on targeted transport corridors. The project also supported Pillar 3: expanding opportunities by reducing inequality for ethnic minorities. The project continues to be relevant to Focus Area 1 (Objective 3) of the current World Bank strategy for Viet Nam: enhance trade competitiveness, multi-modal transport connectivity, and logistics services (CPF for FY18–FY22).2 All of these aspects sought to strengthen economic growth and provide opportunities for the project beneficiaries. Theory of Change (Results Chain) 7. A theory of change (ToC) was not required at the time of project appraisal.

Figure 1 showed the retrospective ToC developed by the Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) team based on the project development objective (PDO), project description, and Results Framework.3 The restructuring in December 2020 did not affect the ToC, and it sought to address issues of (i) inadequate planning for road maintenance due to insufficient data on road condition—this aligns with PDO section on ‘improve the efficiency and sustainability of the national road asset management’; (ii) use of relatively costly traditional contractual arrangements for road—this aligns with the PDO section on ‘sustainability of maintenance practices’; and (iii) formally framing as an outcome the reduced travel times resulting from improved road surfaces, especially along the roads maintained under the Project. 8. The long-term outcome in the project areas was to improve the efficiency and sustainability of road asset management and improve the efficiency and sustainability of road maintenance practices. This aims to improve connectivity and economic activities for the communities along the road corridors and across regional borders. To achieve this long-term objective would require increasing the use of the road asset management database to plan and prioritize transport connectivity on the national network, preserve infrastructural assets, increase accessibility to roads and bridges, strengthen capacity for management of PBCs, and finance road infrastructure.

The project development objective is to improve the efficiency and sustainability of the road asset management and maintenance practices performed by the Ministry of Transport (MOT) on national roads in Viet Nam.4 Key Expected Outcomes and Outcome Indicators 10. The project has been designed to achieve the PDO through a two-pronged approach: PDO outcome 1: Improving efficiency and sustainability of Road Asset Management Practices. This is to be achieved through Component A (establishment of RAMs, increasing financing for road maintenance, introduction of PBC contracts including through developing enabling legal framework, and so forth) and Component D (institutional strengthening, capacity building, and so forth). The achievements are to be measured through the following outcome/output indicators: • Roads rehabilitated in good or fair condition as a share of total classified roads.

SIGNIFICANT CHANGES DURING IMPLEMENTATION (IF APPLICABLE) 12. A level two restructuring was approved in December 2020 to scale up and extend the closing date of the project by 24 months, up to December 31, 2022. The project benefited from savings in the amount of US$ 55.07 million due to the competitive procurement processes and the GoV still provided its counterpart financing notwithstanding the savings. Additional activities introduced into the project included: (i) pavement (road surface) strengthening and intersections of 7.7 km section of NH6 under component B; (ii) construction of a 19.5 km bypass in Son La city under NH2; (iii) improvement and expansion of 1.39 km NH2 under Component C.

These changes introduced during project implementation were beneficial, with output directly linked to the PDO. 13. Additional cost savings in the amount of US$ 21.64 million from procurement processes led to including under the project activities the rehabilitation of NH9 (13.9 km) without a formal restructuring or amendment to the Financing Agreement. The addition of NH9’s 13.8 km road section from Cua Viet port to NH1. This additional activity was requested from the GoV and agreed by the Bank. A decision was reached not to amend the FA to finance this work because the legal agreement was flexible in its language. Rehabilitation of NH9 was not implemented and by Project closing the unused funds for this activity were refunded to the Bank and the scope of work was cancelled from the project and all contracts related to NH9 (including construction, supervision) were terminated except the design contract was completed. Revised PDO Indicators and Outcome Targets 14. The PDO indicators were not formally revised. Some targets were included in the scale-up—a total of 20.89 km of roads added to NH6 (19.5 km), and NH2 (1.39 km). The results framework targets were revised to include the additional roads and they were monitored during project implementation (see Annex 1). RELEVANCE OF PDOs 17. The project objective is aligned with the World Bank Group Country Partnership Framework (CPF) FY18 –22.5 The PDO is still a development priority and issue relevant to Objective 2 of the CPF’s Focus Area 1, ‘Promoting private sector and agri-business development’; and Focus Area 3, 'Enhance trade competitiveness and multi-modal transport connectivity and logistics services in Viet Nam’. To improve the efficiency and sustainability of road asset management, RAMS has been developed: a successful and well-functioning platform which produced accurate information on road asset management. To enhance data integrity, security, data entry accuracy and operational effectiveness, DRVN and PMU staff capacity were enhanced. The project financed data collection equipment including vehicles and customized software for collecting data on the NHs network and analysis by professionals for decision-making. The system utilizes a cloud computing platform to combine and share data from various existing systems, such as the Pavement Management System (PMS) funded by JICA, and the Bridge Management System (VBMS) funded by DRVN. The centralized system supported the nationwide rollout of the new system to monitor and analyze conditions on the NH road network.

At inception, to establish the database, 1,148 items of data were broken down into general information, statistics, inspection, repair history, and property value. The centralized system also added data on 33 different NH assets of the NH network and their attributes, such as road surface conditions and bridges, over several years in order of priority for maintenance planning to ensure the sustainability and preservation of the structural Page 11 of 64 The World Bank Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) integrity of Viet Nam’s national highway network.8 This allowed for efficiency and transparency in planning, annual budget allocation, the prioritization of investment, and maintenance of the national road network. 24. RAMS is connected to the public road network assets system managed by the Ministry of Finance (MoF) and has created unit costs and cost norms for maintenance and management. During the project implementation, DRVN issued regulations on management, operation, and exploration of RAMS. The system provides information for continued piloting of maintenance planning for roads, bridges and 32 other assets for some routes under Regional Road Management Bureaus (RRMBs).

Given the excellent performance of RAMS, at the time of closing the system is the nationwide method used for evaluating pavement conditions—and more importantly, this has meant that DRVN and Provincial Departments of Transport (PDoTs) across the country have been able to access data on road conditions for planning and budgeting. 25. Expansion of PBC program in national road maintenance. PBC contracts are quite new in Viet Nam compared to the traditional method of road maintenance. Over the past 20 years prior to the project, the government has tried to introduce the PBC model with little success. VRAMP succeeded in piloting a PBC roll out. The groundwork involved establishing the regulatory system for PBC contracts (including regulatory framework, standard bidding documents and PBC supervision manual, plus training to build the institutional capacity of relevant agencies and contractors) and research to compare the effectiveness of different maintenance methods to ensure effective implementation. The project financed and implemented 234 km of roads under PBC maintenance contracts for NH6 for 48 months and for NH2 for 60 months. Based on the successful results of PBC maintenance in the project, DRVN has expanded the PBC model for the maintenance of whole National Highway network. 26. KEY FACTORS DURING PREPARATION 47. Project objective and strategic direction. The objectives of VRAMP were highly relevant, given the challenges facing Viet Nam in terms of managing road assets. The project was a follow-on to the (now closed) RNIP and drew lessons from it on the importance of improved maintenance practices. MOT, DRVN and PMU3’s capacity was enhanced to manage PBCs and the national road network, and to establish the Road Asset Management Framework through a study tour on PBCs (to Brazil) and on PPP (to India, China, and Malaysia). The selection of priority sites and bridges was based on sound criteria. The initial sequencing of tasks and timing was appropriate, as it focused on PBCs and the maintenance of networks for better connectivity from the provinces to urban centers. The procurement processes ensured 30 percent of bidding documents were prepared and available by project negotiations. The project had a high level of readiness for implementation, after Board approval. Page 19 of 64 The World Bank Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) 49. Implementation arrangement. The World Bank conducted an internal appraisal process and confirmed that the additional work was feasible and that it was justifiable to finance NH9 improvement under VRAMP within the 16-month period left for implementation.

This was admittedly ambitious, but consideration was given because (i) Quang Tri province had been performing very well to implement WB projects over the prior 20 years (that is, RTP1, 2, 3 and LRAMP); (ii) Quang Tri’s LAR was relatively small and uncomplicated, compared with the one from Son La province, where LAR and construction were completed within two years. Quang Tri failed to execute the LARs due to the increased cost of LAR (a five-fold increase) even though MOT/DRVN/PMU3 put in an extraordinary effort to accelerate the bidding and launch of works and consultant contracts within eight months of the Project Investment Plan (PIP) being approved for NH9. However, MOT’s efforts were jeopardized by LAR failure and Quang Tri province underestimating the cost of LAR at the time of this ICR. BANK PERFORMANCE, COMPLIANCE ISSUES, AND RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME A. QUALITY OF MONITORING AND EVALUATION (M&E) M&E Design 61. DRVN and PMU3 were responsible for monitoring results and activities. A dedicated M&E unit in DRVN, PMU3, the Supervision consultant and designated staff in the provinces contributed to ensuring data availability and collection at all levels of implementation. The Project procured modern road surface condition data collection devices which were compatible with the PMS system and supported DRVN with data collection and processing of images obtained from CCTV cameras, surface crack detection using the international roughness index (IRI), road surface settlement, surveys, and geographic coordinates. The overall results framework was appropriate for measuring the achievements of the project outcomes and outputs. The linkage between the intermediate results indicators and the PDO outcomes was measurable. However, some indicators were not attributable to the project. The PDO indicators on Roads Rehabilitated targets were not attributable to the project and therefore cannot serve to verify that the entire NH Network has been rehabilitated during the project, over and above measuring the conditions of the network and action plan for rehabilitation. This project built on and expanded support from previous World Bank financed projects in Viet Nam in an area that remains relevant and strategic to the country’s efforts to improve connectivity from the national level to the provinces. Infrastructure development through the improvement and maintenance of the existing national road network is key to achieving sustainable and inclusive development. The project supported Viet Nam at a critical time when other donors, including the ADB and JICA, sought to strengthen RAMS through the development of software as a tool for the analysis of preservation options, planning and direct investment in infrastructure maintenance. The use of PBCs (which were relatively new in Viet Nam at the time) optimized the process of road asset management, resulting in increased usage of PBCs, coupled with training, specialized capacity development, and ownership by MOT, DRVN, PMU3, and the provinces. 76. GoV support to the established RAMS. Broadly speaking, the GoV’s efforts to preserve the RAMS have a high likelihood of continued expansion on the achievement of the PDO. The RAMS, if used effectively, is expected to produce reliable data that will enhance GoV decisions regarding the maintenance of the NH corridors constructed under the project and beyond. The RAMS/RAMF are updated by staff (who received RAMS training and certificate) from DRVN and PDoTs. DRVN had faced financial difficulties in maintaining the virtual servers and Wi-Fi services but has allocated its own budget while waiting for official allocation from MOT. Capacity already built within DRVN/PMU3 on PBC is to be sustained. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 83. Ownership, support, and leadership at the National and Provincial level were critical to success. At the National level, there was sustained ownership under the leadership of the Ministry of Transportation (MOT) and strong leadership by DRVN and PMU3, the implementing agency. This ensured continued growth in financing to accommodate the project needs. These efforts need to be sustained. At the provincial level, there was strong support for and Page 27 of 64 The World Bank Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) understanding of the project by PPCs, who engaged regularly with key local stakeholders and beneficiaries in relation to resettlement and road sections within their jurisdiction. This resulted in successful completion of activities. These committees should be strengthened and their experiences showcased as those of exemplary results-oriented achievers. The structures and relationships formed in the districts—as well as the local leadership—were fundamental to the success of the project. 84. Sustainability and institutionalization of the Road Asset Management System (RAMS). The establishment of the RAMS is a positive impact to maintain sustainability of transport assets in Viet Nam and a global example of planning for road maintenance. Through technological advances, the new system with its unique software produced timely data conducive to reliable responses in upgrading of the road network.

One of the most significant achievements of RAMS is an effective planning tool linked to the government’s existing road and asset management systems that brings together relevant National Highways and Provincial roads data. The road management agencies are empowered to generate periodic data reports, planning for maintenance, and upgrading of the road network. The innovations and transparent operations of RAMS have evolved to become one of the largest data collection systems in Viet Nam. As a result, the RAMS model has been adopted by other Ministries for issuance of driver’s licenses, and monitoring trucking overload, among other purposes. 85. PBCs are crucial for successful implementation and sustainability of road maintenance. The 234km maintained by the project under the PBC method along NH 2 and NH 6 effected a move away from traditional road construction. This was key for maintaining excellent road surface, traffic safety and drainage, allowing for smooth and steady traffic for five years after the contracts had expired. Exposure to global practices aimed at sustaining technical skills on the concepts of PBC proved vital for promoting long-term maintenance of high-quality roads in the future. At the policy level, following the results of this robust innovation, PBC is being decentralized and expanded across Viet Nam for the maintenance and repair of National Highways. 86.

Efficient and timely payment of compensation for resettlement and land acquisition is critical for project implementation. Delays in resettlement are a systemic challenge encountered in the Viet Nam country portfolio. The World Bank and the GoV are working to address these issues. Under the project, land acquisition and resettlement ended up requiring five times more than the original budget allocation. Current market prices and land price increases had not been foreseen, and implementation delays were the consequence. This project's experience has demonstrated the need to closely monitor and prepare for price adjustment scale during implementation and request the appropriate allocation as needed. A land price agreement and prompt payment of compensation would lessen the effects of rising land prices and implementation delays. 87. Adding new activities to a well-performing project should be carefully analyzed, especially given a long LAR implementation period. In the context of this project, the additional activities were ambitious considering the capacity of the implementing agency, the financial constraints of the PPC, and time left for implementation without extension. When discussing additional activities, in-depth assessment, selectivity, clearly defined activities with timeline and risk mitigation measures should be factored in to provide a clear view of what is possible to be accomplished within the time left before project closing. .

KEY ISSUES & STATUS 4.1 Implementation Status and Key Decisions Progress towards achievement of the Project Development Objective (PDO) is on track, with all PDO indicators (6) having met the target. A total of 1,222 km of road receiving routine maintenance (PBC) has been completed in six project provinces. All 11 contracts (1,574.46 km) for the second three-year period (2023 – 2025) are under implementation, with physical progress at around 46-93%. For National Road 13 South (NR13S), roadworks has been under the operation and maintenance (O&M) phase. The Technical Assistance (TA) and institutional strengthening activities are almost completed. However, it is important to utilize the technical tools provided under the project (i.e., RMS, PRoMMS, IRAMS-2) to "modernize" MPWT's business process, especially with MPWT's staff shortage issue becoming more critical. There remains a need to address and improve on counterpart funding, overloading control, and road safety implementation. 5. There remains a need to address and improve on counterpart funding, overloading control, and road safety implementation. 5. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL CONTEXT 1. At appraisal in 2016, Lao PDR had sustained strong economic growth, averaging around 8 percent annually since 2000, driven by natural resources, infrastructure investment, and tourism. Although poverty had declined significantly, it remained concentrated in remote and ethnic minority areas. To support continued growth and rural development, the Government sought to improve regional and domestic connectivity as part of its strategy to transform Lao PDR from a landlocked to a land-linked economy. 2. Road transport was the backbone of the economy, carrying about 98 percent of passenger traffic and 96 percent of freight. However, the road network was increasingly affected by recurrent flooding and other climate-related events, which caused significant damage, expanded maintenance backlogs, and increased reliance on costly emergency repairs. Provincial and district roads were particularly vulnerable due to lower design standards, inadequate maintenance, and limited consideration of climate risks in infrastructure design. 3.

Fiscal constraints, inadequate road resilience, and weak maintenance capacity posed significant challenges to the sustainability of the road network. Frequent climate-related damage further strained limited resources and increased reconstruction, recovery and maintenance costs. Although road asset management systems had been established for both national and provincial roads —including the Road Management System (RMS) and the Provincial Road Maintenance Management System (PRoMMS), which were introduced progressively in the early to mid-2000s under earlier road sector programs—their effectiveness was constrained by weak data, limited integration of climate risk considerations, competing investment priorities, and capacity constraints at subnational levels. 4. To address these constraints and promote inclusive growth and economic diversification, the Government of Lao People’s Democratic Republic (GoL) sought financing from the World Bank for Lao Road Sector Project II (LRSP2) to improve resilience of road network, reduce recurring disaster recovery costs, and strengthen institutional capacity to maintain road reliability. The project was designed to anchor a broader sector-wide approach, with the World Bank serving as the lead financing and coordinating partner and the Nordic Development Fund (NFD) as co-financier.

LRSP2 intentionally leveraged financing for the European Investment Bank (EIB), the European Union (EU), and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), and Government road sector funding to enhance road network resilience, accessibility, and sustainability across the road sector as a whole within prioritized rural areas with high vulnerability to climate risks. To achieve these objectives, LRSP2 prioritized investment in disaster-prone rural areas in northern Lao PDR including Phongsaly, Houaphan, Oudomxay, Xiengkhouang, Xayabouly and Bolikhamxay provinces, where recurrent flash floods and slope failures frequently disrupted road connectivity. 5. LRSP2 built on the achievements of the Lao Road Sector Project (LRSP; P102398, 2010-2016). LRSP improved road conditions, established road asset management systems, strengthened road sector institutions, and enhanced rural connectivity (World Bank, 2022: 45)1. Expanding on these foundations, LRSP2 adopted a more systematic approach by integrating climate-resilient periodic maintenance into national and subnational road management systems and introducing a Contingency Emergency Response Component (CERC). The project also served as a platform for collaboration among development partners under the sector-wide approach, supporting harmonized investments and policy reforms across the road sector. LRSP2 was aligned with the World Bank’s Country Partnership Strategy for the 1 World Bank. 2022.

LRSP2 comprised four components to strengthen road maintenance systems at both the national and provincial/district levels, contributing to improved road reliability. LRSP2 was designed to mainstream best practices by implementing a sector-wide approach to addressing the full range of road maintenance challenges through the existing government institutional structure under the coordination of a Project Coordination Committee (PCC). Component 1 focused on enhancing maintenance systems at provincial and district levels, whereas Components 2 and 3 strengthened institutional capacities and project management functions across the entire road sector. By incorporating climate resilience as a cross-cutting element under Components 2 and 4, the project also helped the Government better prepare for—and respond to—potential road damage and service disruptions caused by climate-related disasters. ACHIEVEMENT OF PDOs (EFFICACY) ASSESSMENT OF ACHIEVEMENT OF EACH OBJECTIVE/OUTCOME 23. Changes to the PDO and outcome targets in 2019 made the project more ambitious (see paragraph 11). Assessment of efficacy is organized around the four project objectives: [PDO 1] improve climate resilience, [PDO 2] strengthen maintenance systems, and [PDO 3] provide an immediate response to an eligible crisis or emergency. PDO 1 – To improve Climate Resilience of the road network 24. PDO 1 was substantially achieved based on World Bank–financed interventions, including climate resilient periodic maintenance (656 km), routine maintenance under performance-based contracts (1,574 km), and the rehabilitation and OPBRC-based operation and maintenance of NR13 South.

These interventions contributed to improvements in provincial and district road conditions within supported network segments, reflected in the increase in the share of roads in good or fair condition from 50 to 67 percent. Improvement in drainage, slope stabilization, and timely maintenance are associated with enhanced resilience to climate-related disruptions. 25. These results were driven primarily by performance‑based contracting modalities, which introduced service‑level requirements for continuous maintenance and monitoring. In particular, the OPBRC approach aligned contractor incentives with lifecycle performance, supporting more sustained management of climate-related risks. These performance‑based maintenance and rehabilitation activities were further supported by risk‑based planning approaches developed under the project, which guided the prioritization of interventions based on field survey data integrated into RMS and PRoMMS (see paragraphs 29-31). 26. Climate events disrupted parts of the road network which had not yet been improved by the project, and required reprioritization of maintenance, contributing to reduced routine maintenance outputs (1,570 km achieved against a revised target of 1,960 km).

Despite this adjustment, project-supported climate-resilient maintenance continued to sustain road condition and serviceability, as reflected in achievement of the PDO indicators, including an estimated 2.134 million beneficiaries, indicating strengthened resilience and connectivity under adverse conditions. 27. Beyond these directly attributable outcomes, LRSP2 supported climate‑resilient road improvements through the broader sector‑wide approach in which IDA-supported approaches helped align Development Partner financing and government funding for the road sector in the project area. By scaling-up both use of performance‑based contracts and integrating climate resilience into prioritization, design, and works, LRSP2 anchored and led Development Partner support for the road sector overall including both NR13 South and climate-resilient provincial road improvements implemented under mixed financing arrangements. The sector-wide framework supported robust approaches to contract supervision, quality assurance, and technical standards, contributing to the quality of outcomes beyond the scope of the project’s direct financing. 28. Interpretation of the results requires clear attribution, given that rehabilitation outcomes were delivered through a sector-wide approach involving multiple financing sources. Under the sector-wide approach, LRSP2 would rehabilitate 58 km of NR13 S, while Development Partners would rehabilitate the remaining 217 km.

For example, IDA financing supported the conceptual design for all of NR13S and NDF financing supported design and supervision for provincial and district roads. At the system level, LRSP2 contributed to strengthening of maintenance practices by operationalizing maintenance systems and coordinating government implementation and development partner support to align with improved technical approaches.

The project was built on asset management systems RMS and PRoMMS introduced under the prior World Bank-supported operation to dramatically enhance their impact. This included the adoption of three‑year rolling plans, integration of climate and risk data, the expanded use of performance‑based contracting, including use of asset management systems for government planning and budgeting. 32. Taken together, these interventions strengthened maintenance planning and its operationalization. Integration of risk-based asset management into maintenance planning, including the Transport Sector Five-Year Plan (2026–2030), continued use of RMS/PRoMMS within the government’s medium-term planning and budgeting framework, and mainstreaming of PBC contracting and design standards resulted in a sustained strengthening of maintenance systems. C. EFFICIENCY 36. Economic efficiency and use of resources exceeded norms in the road sector in Lao PDR. Project management and implementation were efficient, with no major delays or cost overruns despite numerous challenges such as the COVID-19 pandemic, high inflation, and adoption of a complex road works contracting approach (OPBRC). 37. The ex-post economic evaluation found the project’s economic efficiency slightly exceeded the appraisal forecast, reflecting higher-than-expected avoided damage from more severe climate events and stronger-than-forecast traffic on NR13 South.

For World Bank–financed activities, the Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) was 31.5 percent (NPV: US$19.95 million) for local road improvement and maintenance (Components 1.1 and 1.2), and 34.4 percent (NPV: US$37.8 million) for Section 1 of NR13 South. Key economic benefits of the local road improvement and maintenance are from lower vehicle operating costs (VOC), improved access for local populations, and reduced emergency repair costs. For NR13 South, benefits include lower VOCs, reduced travel time, reduced emergency repair costs, value of time savings from freight delays, and reduced impacts of road crashes (see Annex 4). 38. Under the parallel financing structure, overall results for NR13 South—including sections financed by development partners—achieved an EIRR of 33.9 percent (NPV: US$212.46 million). While these aggregated results reflect the combined contributions of multiple financiers, the World Bank-financed sections demonstrate comparable or higher returns, particularly for NR13 South, indicating strong economic performance within the scope of IDA-supported interventions. 39. Use of resources for LRSP2 implementation was highly efficient. LRSP2 responded to multiple shocks during implementation, including tropical storm Son Tinh, the global COVID-19 pandemic, and tropical storms and floods in 2023 through 2025.

Critically, the sector-wide approach reduced administrative costs as a single PMU was utilized for implementation of all Development Partner support to the road sector. While an extension of the project closing date was required, the additional implementation period enabled a large scaling-up of impact to include rehabilitation of 275 km of NR13 S under the sector wide engagement. The project delivered strong benefits for women who accounted for approximately half of the 2,888,000 direct beneficiaries. The project played a meaningful role in creating employment opportunities for women and strengthening gender inclusion in a traditionally male-dominated sector through its maintenance and contracting arrangements. Starting from a baseline of zero in 2016, the share of women employed in project-related paid work increased steadily with the expansion of routine maintenance and performance-based contracts, reaching about 17–18 percent by 2023, well above the end target of 10 percent.

INSTITUTIONAL STRENGTHENING 43. LRSP2 strengthened institutional capacity for road maintenance and asset management by embedding risk-based planning, performance-based contracting, and climate resilience considerations into routine sector practices. Through RMS and PRoMMS, maintenance planning became more systematic and evidence-based, while training and on-the-job learning enhanced the capacity of government agencies, consultants, and contractors. These efforts helped institutionalize a more proactive, lifecycle-based approach to road asset management and supported the long-term sustainability of sector reforms. MOBILIZING PRIVATE SECTOR FINANCING 44. The OPBRC implemented on NR13 South mobilized private sector pre‑financing for initial rehabilitation and repairs. This was enabled by integrating design and construction with long‑term operations and maintenance (O&M), and by adopting a structure under which a portion of capital expenditure (approximately 20 percent) is repaid during the O&M period, conditional on sustained performance. Under the OPBRC, private pre‑financing helped reduce the government’s upfront fiscal burden and smooth expenditures over time, while creating strong incentives for timely completion and quality assurance, particularly in a context of macroeconomic volatility.

In this respect, LRSP2 demonstrated the feasibility of a contracting approach that combines performance accountability with fiscal sustainability under constrained public financing conditions. 45. In addition, the successful implementation of the NR13 S OPBRC informed the preparation of the following CRRCIP. Rather than assuming an automatic expansion of OPBRC, CRRCIP builds on the institutional, capacity, and financing experience accumulated under LRSP2, with a focus on creating the conditions for the gradual extension of OPBRC where appropriate. Within Lao PDR, OPBRC is a scalable contracting model that can be selectively applied, subject to the suitability of road sections and the availability of enabling fiscal and institutional conditions. POVERTY REDUCTION AND SHARED PROSPERITY 46. The project contributed to poverty reduction by improving accessibility and mobility in project areas. The beneficiary assessment conducted during the Mid-Term Review Mission (November 23–December 4, 2020) suggests that reductions in travel time and transport costs were likely to generate positive spillover effects over the longer term, including increased income-earning opportunities and expanded economic activity. In addition, the institutionalization of risk-based maintenance planning supported a shift toward more preventive and predictable maintenance, reducing reliance on reactive and costly emergency repairs.

By easing this fiscal pressure on the road sector, the project helped improve the reliability of all-season roads and, indirectly, supported greater access to economic opportunities over time. OTHER UNINTENDED OUTCOMES AND IMPACTS 47. LRSP2 generated positive downstream effects beyond the PDOs. The project-financed axel load control study identified key limitations of traditional weigh-station-based enforcement, including evasion risks, corruption exposure, and increased logistics costs due to vehicle stopping requirements, leading to introduction of weigh-in-motion (WIM)-based alternatives for network-level monitoring and screening of heavy vehicles. The subsequent installation of WIM systems strengthened data-driven overloading control and supported more targeted and transparent enforcement 9 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT practices and led to consideration of road user fee mechanisms to support long-term maintenance. These institutional improvements enhanced the basis for protecting road assets beyond the project’s original results framework. Such user fee mechanisms, still under consideration, may further enhance sustainability of the road sector. III. KEY FACTORS AFFECTING IMPLEMENTATION AND OUTCOME A. KEY FACTORS DURING PREPARATION 48.

Project preparation drew on lessons from LRSP and incorporated measures to strengthen readiness, including stakeholder consultations, clarified institutional roles through Memorandum of Understanding (MoUs) between MPWT and DPWTs, and procurement and financial management capacity assessments. A road survey mission also informed the design of climate resilience interventions. Building on the systems and foundations established under LRSP, LRSP2 prioritized climate resilience, improved data quality, and strengthened decentralized implementation. 49. LRSP2 Preparation continued the World Bank-led sector-wide, multi-donor engagement approach of LRSP. Facilitating alignment among NDF, EIB, and the EU leveraged IDA financing for greater impact. Following joint needs assessments, the World Bank supported the identification of priority investments and initial financing, with partners collaborating as a single program with unified implementation arrangements (including a shared PMU) and clearly delineating responsibilities across partners based on implementation capacity. Coordination extended to use of common design standards and bidding documents, effectively streamlining best practice into government systems. B. KEY FACTORS DURING IMPLEMENTATION Factors Subject to Government and Implementing Entity Control 50. Coordination and engagement.

The Project Coordination Committee (PCC) coordinated central and provincial government entities effectively within the decentralization context in which central agencies were responsible for strategic planning, budgeting, and system management, and provincial authorities led implementation of maintenance activities. The PCC supported coordination among key MPWT departments— including Department of Roads (DOR), Department of Planning and Finance (DPF), Department of Transport (DOT), and Environmental and Disaster Prevention Division (EDPD)—while the Project Management Unit (PMU) facilitated regular communication and issue resolution. Differences in local capacity and the evolving nature of coordination arrangements influenced the pace and consistency of implementation across provinces. 51. Human resources and organizational capacity. Deployment of specialized consultants and extensive technical assistance supported capacity building in performance‑based contracting (PBC and OPBRC), road safety and technical audits, financial and procurement management, and the operationalization of ICT tools such as PRoMMS, RMS, and IRAM-2, as well as road safety data systems. 52. Strong government ownership. The GoL took proactive regulatory and planning actions to operationalize and institutionalize reforms introduced during implementation, drawing on technical assistance provided by the World Bank.

The authorities updated and approved the national Road Safety Strategy and Action Plan and established a three-year rolling maintenance planning process, as an annually updated requirement. Factors Subject to World Bank Control 53. Proactive implementation support. The World Bank provided close and structured implementation support through regular missions and sustained technical and fiduciary oversight, with a focus on works quality, performance-based maintenance contracts, and environmental and social safeguards. During implementation, the 10 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT DLI-based results framework was discontinued, and supervision accordingly placed greater emphasis on performance monitoring and quality assurance within the existing PBC framework. Supervision findings informed follow-up actions, including targeted guidance, capacity-building support, and training on contract management and quality assurance. The World Bank also provided analytical input and technical assistance on overloading control, which contributed to subsequent government consideration of a more system-level approach to overloading management. 54. Pandemic crisis management and adaptive implementation support. LRSP2 maintained implementation continuity through adaptive management in the face of unanticipated shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic, climate-related disasters, and macroeconomic instability and inflation.

The World Bank proactively supported the response to Tropical Storm Son Tinh, transition to remote implementation support, and contract management in response to post-pandemic inflation (see paragraphs 56-58) through restructuring, contract-agreed price adjustments, rebalancing PBC contracts with extended routine maintenance, and strengthened payment processing and coordination. 55. Development Partner coordination. Successful coordination with Development Partners facilitated additional parallel financing for NR13 S under the sector-wide approach at the time of the 2019 AF, scaling up LRSP2 far beyond initial expectations. The World Bank’s leading and coordinating role mobilized resources for rehabilitation of 275 km of NR13 S through project and parallel financing resources. While IDA financed rehabilitation of 40 km (km 71-111) of NR13 S, EIB financed 157 km (km 111-190 and km 267-346); and AIIB financed the final 78 km (km 190- 268). Factors Outside the Control of Government and Implementing Entities 56. Typhoon Son-Tinh. Severe flooding and extreme rainfall associated with Typhoon Son-Tinh in 2018 caused widespread road damage requiring emergency repair and recovery needs that exceeded the assumptions and resources of the original project design, resulting in the 2018 Restructuring and 2019 Additional Financing. 57. COVID-19 and post-pandemic macroeconomic instability.

COVID-19 related travel restrictions limited the deployment of international consultants, postponed training and capacity-building activities (including Environmental, Social, Health and Safety (ESHS) and Occupational Health and Safety (OHS)) and resulted in challenging remote implementation support. While economic fallout of the pandemic – combined with already high national debt – led to rising inflation and reduced the purchasing power of the RMF counterpart financing, IDA- financed works contracts continued to perform effectively. 58. Additional climate events including Yagi and Wipa. Recurrent climate events late in implementation resulted in the need for additional repairs on critical road links and shifting some RMF resources away from routine maintenance. The combination of inflation and these emergency repairs meant that RMF counterpart financing could only finance 1,574.46 km of routine maintenance, short of the revised target of 1,960. IV. BANK PERFORMANCE, COMPLIANCE ISSUES, AND RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME A. QUALITY OF MONITORING AND EVALUATION (M&E) M&E Design 59. Overall, the M&E design articulates three project objectives and six well-designed PDO indicators to capture project area outcomes.

Monitoring the preparation of the three-year rolling maintenance plans at the PDO-level is strategic indicator to demonstrate that both MPWT and DPWT consider climate vulnerability and road infrastructure conditions (including factors affecting resilience) maintenance and budgeting process. After 2018 flood events revealed 11 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT structural limitations of the DLI for hybrid PBC contracts, the 2019 Additional Financing removed the DLI and strengthened supervision-based performance monitoring through enhanced technical oversight (see paragraphs 14 and 19). One shortcoming in M&E design is that the end target for the percentage of the rural population in the project area with access to all-season road could have been increased in 2019 to reflect the addition of NR13 South to the project scope. 60. Intermediate indicators provided a structured basis for monitoring implementation progress and institutional outcomes. They captured social inclusion, and governance aspects such as women’s participation in road‑related employment, community involvement in maintenance monitoring, and grievance redress performance. They also tracked the institutional mainstreaming of road safety and climate risk management through road safety audits. M&E Implementation 61. Project M&E implementation utilized institutionalized road data collection and road maintenance management software effectively.

Monitoring systems—anchored in RMS and PRoMMS—were complemented by provincial data collection, central review processes, and independent verification through technical audits and field inspections. Data on road condition, quality, and safety were regularly collected through Road Safety Audits, annual technical audits, and inspections conducted by MPWT and DPWT. Data quality was sufficient for supporting prioritization and oversight, although provincial quality control processes can be improved. Monitoring of environmental, social, and inclusion aspects was carried out effectively through institutionalized data collection mechanisms, Community Participatory Monitoring (CPM), the Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM), and employment records. M&E Utilization 62. M&E data was actively used to track progress toward results and improve performance. Data on road condition and natural-hazard vulnerability collected through ICT-based M&E systems, including PRoMMS, were used to identify priority sections for Climate Resilient Periodic Maintenance, enabling the strategic allocation of limited resources to the most vulnerable road segments. PBC, OPBRC, and independent technical audits strengthened continuous oversight and accountability for maintenance outcomes through regular checks against contract-specific service levels and performance standards, field validation, and performance confirmation linked to payment certification.

Information generated through CPM, the GRM, environmental and social safeguards monitoring, and the indicator on women’s employment in road works contracts was used to identify implementation risks early and support proactive corrective actions, including adjustments to contract implementation, field-level remedial measures, and enhanced supervision. Justification of Overall Rating of Quality of M&E 63. Substantial. There were at most moderate shortcomings due to the need to drop the DLI. B. ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND FIDUCIARY COMPLIANCE 64. The project was initially classified as Category A and triggered following safeguard policies: Environmental Assessment OP/BP 4.01, Natural Habitats OP/BP 4.04, Forests OP/BP 4.36, Physical Cultural Resources OP/BP 4.11, Indigenous Peoples OP/BP 4.10, and Involuntary Resettlement OP/BP 4.12. The project required the preparation of an Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF), including a generic Environmental Codes of Practice (ECoP) and an outline Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP). Given that road interventions would be identified during implementation, a framework approach was adopted.

MPWT prepared and disclosed an Environmental and Social Management Framework (ESMF), a Resettlement Policy Framework (RPF) and an Ethnic Groups Policy Framework (EGPF) considering related GoL regulations including the Environmental and Social Operations Manual (ESOM) and experience gained with safeguard implementation on a prior road project in Lao PDR. English versions were re-disclosed on the World Bank website on July 27, 2016. In 2019, the project was reclassified to Category B. Environmental and social safeguard requirements were implemented without major exceptions, 12 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT including for large‑scale works, supported by effective grievance redress mechanisms. Procurement and financial management systems were largely compliant with World Bank requirements. C. BANK PERFORMANCE Quality at Entry 65. The World Bank’s performance at entry was satisfactory. At the appraisal stage, the project design was well aligned with Lao PDR’s road sector priorities and Development Partners. The design placed appropriate emphasis on sustainability by prioritizing road maintenance over new construction and by integrating climate resilience considerations into planning and implementation and addressed critical institutional and capacity challenges of weak maintenance systems, limited asset management capacity, and decentralization. 66.

LRSP2 benefited from a strong understanding of Lao PDR’s road sector constraints and institutional context , building on the foundations established under the original LRSP. LRSP2 continued and deepened strategic sector reforms for improving road network performance by addressing persistent limitations in road asset management capacity and contracting. The project established a coherent direction for strengthening sector institutions across the full maintenance cycle, from systematic road data collection and condition surveys to maintenance planning, prioritization, and oversight arrangements, thereby supporting a more structured and performance-oriented approach to road management. 67. The leading role played by the World Bank in Lao PDR’s road sector enabled it to effectively leverage parallel financing and counterpart financing to expand LRSP2s reach as a consolidated sector-wide reform agenda. Anchoring LRSP2 reforms in government asset management and budgetary processes reinforced Government ownership and promoted institutionalization of maintenance planning, technical standards, and oversight across Development Partners. While reliance on counterpart financing—including RMF resources— exposed the project to macroeconomic risks, including RMF co-financing enhanced the project’s impact. 68. Rating: Satisfactory Quality of Supervision 69.

The World Bank provided performance-oriented and adaptive implementation support for the sector-wide engagement throughout LRSP2 implementation. In the parallel financing environment, implementation support was undertaken from a system-level perspective encompassing the full road asset management framework, including maintenance execution, PBC/OPBRC performance, fiduciary and procurement management, environmental and social safeguards, road safety, and asset management systems. The World Bank maintained active coordination with Development Partners on the scope of road works and successfully promoted adoption of the World Bank OPBRC bidding documents under financing from the AIIB and EIB. Use of common technical standards and performance requirements likewise reinforced government ownership and helped deepen reforms. 70. Supervision was adapted to multiple shocks, including COVID-19 and recurrent floods; the World Bank used M&E evidence to adjust performance management instruments. Implementation support was highly responsive to client needs, including the decision to drop the DLI in favor of performance-based contracting supported by independent technical audits, preparation of additional financing, and support to respond to inflation. 71. From a sustainability perspective, supervision increasingly addressed structural risks to long-term road performance.

The implementation of the Overloading Control Study, the reactivation of weight control stations, and the introduction of WIM equipment on selected sections were monitored as part of supervision. These measures helped prevent premature road deterioration and stabilize maintenance outcomes. Supervision also considered financial sustainability, including maintenance financing through the Road Fund and the medium- to long-term consideration of 13 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT demand and revenue management options, including toll systems, thereby extending the supervision focus beyond project closure. 72. Rating: Satisfactory Justification of Overall Rating of Bank Performance 73. Overall Bank performance is rated Satisfactory D. RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME 74. The project’s success significantly strengthening road maintenance systems has contributed to the sustainability of the road network improvements financed by the project. LRSP2 has substantially strengthened these systems asset management systems and OPBRC‑based maintenance practices within MPWT and DPWTs and the GoL continues to show strong commitment to these. Long-term sustainability of these road maintenance systems and the network depends upon stable macroeconomic conditions. 75.

The Government is continuing efforts to strengthen the sustainability of road maintenance financing through tolling and overloading charges and factoring road maintenance expenditures into the medium-term fiscal framework. While these developments do not fully resolve structural constraints, incremental steps toward improving the sustainability and institutional integration of road maintenance financing demonstrate sustained commitment. Beyond operationalizing maintenance planning and budgeting in the road sector institutions such as the Road Fund, LRSP2 has contributed to institutionalizing maintenance budgeting within the broader Laotian legal frameworks. 76. Risks to network‑level continuity are further reduced by continued parallel financing support for all operation and maintenance of all NR13 S sections under OPBRC. In addition, the preparation of the CRRCIP provides a pathway to scale up maintenance practices, climate resilience standards, and asset management systems beyond LRSP2. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 77. The project showed that performance-based maintenance (PBC/OPBRC), supported by rolling multi-year maintenance planning and road asset management systems, can deliver and sustain improvements in road condition and accessibility when embedded in government decision-making and budget processes.

Integration of climate resilience into road maintenance systems in Lao PDR resulted from a sustained commitment to building institutional, technical, and human capital and institutionalizing maintenance systems among government stakeholders and Development Partners over the past decade. These results would not have been possible without strong and consistent government commitment, sustained engagement of the World Bank and other development partners, and strong task team leadership. 78. Climate resilience proved most effective when mainstreamed across the full maintenance cycle —from design and planning to asset management and execution—resulting in fewer disruptions, lower long-term costs, and more reliable connectivity. Development Partners coordination to promote PBC was a successful strategy to keep the road infrastructure sustainability in the climate vulnerable context of Lao PDR. Rewarding the contractors for regular and timely maintenance ensured maintenance completed which improved the resilience of the road network. Early agreement on common standards, aligned schedules, and a clear coordination framework were essential to fully realize the benefits to rolling out performance-based contracting in the context of parallel financing. 14 The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT 79. The project also highlights that formal emergency response mechanisms such as CERC may not always be the preferred option for governments.

In practice, the ability to respond effectively depended more on operational readiness, including pre-agreed procedures under the ERM and the use of existing contract arrangements. EFFICIENCY ANALYSIS 1. The efficiency analysis for the ICR of the project is based on a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) approach, which follows the same methodology at appraisal stage, including additional financing stage.

The efficiency analysis covers the time horizon of 10 years (2017-2027) for road improvements and maintenance under the original project (Component 1.1 & 1.2) and 20 years (2019-2039) for the OPBRC under Additional Financing (Component 1.5), which are based on the life cycle of actual sub-projects implemented which are road improvement. The project supported the rehabilitation of 64 km of National Road 13 North. The key assumptions include: (i) the discount rate of 12 percent; (ii) the Standard Conversion Factor (SCF) of 0.92 for investment and 0.87 for maintenance; (iii) the project could help avoid some of the emergency maintenance due to the climate resiliency improvement; and (iv) the speed improvement from 47 km/h to 70 km/h on National Roads. 2. At appraisal, the economic internal rate of return (EIRR) for Components 1.1 and 1.2 (local road improvement and maintenance) was estimated at 31.5 percent, with a net present value (NPV) of US$6.85 million. Ex-post analysis conducted in 2026 indicates an EIRR of 31.5 percent and an NPV of US$19.95 million, suggesting that economic returns for local roads were broadly maintained, with higher realized benefits reflected in the increased NPV. 3. For the full 275 km NR13 South corridor, the ex-ante economic analysis conducted under the 2019 Additional Financing estimated an overall EIRR of 26.1 percent and an NPV of US$105.54 million.

At appraisal, the corridor was structured into three sections for analytical purposes, broadly reflecting the parallel financing arrangement across development partners, though not all sections were explicitly assigned to specific financiers. During implementation, the packaging of works was restructured from three into four sections to reflect contractor capacity and facilitate timely delivery, resulting in revised section boundaries and a clearer allocation of financing among IDA, EIB, and AIIB. Ex-post results indicate an EIRR of 34.4 percent and an NPV of US$37.8 million for Section 1 (approximately 40 km) financed under the IDA credit, compared to an overall EIRR of 33.9 percent and an NPV of US$212.46 million for the full NR13S corridor. 4. This distinction reflects the underlying financing structure. While IDA financing supported Section 1 of NR13S, the economic benefits of rehabilitating and operating the full corridor were realized at the aggregate level through coordinated multi-partner implementation. Accordingly, economic efficiency can be assessed both at the level of IDA‑financed investments and at the level of overall corridor outcomes achieved through coordinated multi‑partner implementation. The EIRR at completion (33.9%) is also higher than the level envisioned at AF appraisal due to the higher traffic volume on NR13 S than what was anticipated at appraisal. This provides larger benefits from VOC and VOT savings, and that the economic analysis at appraisal was more conservative with some of the improvement assumptions. While Lao PDR experienced 1-2 major natural disaster events annually in 2010s, the number increased to around 3-4 events in the 2020s. Based on the historical data of MPWT’s emergency maintenance expenses during 2017- 2025, the overall 3-year moving average of the emergency maintenance cost has been reduced by 22%. Taking into account the increasing frequency of natural disaster events, this average emergency maintenance per climate event is estimated to be reduced by 46%.

An analysis of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions was undertaken for NR13 South based on fuel consumption rates at different speeds under ‘with project’ and ‘without project’ scenarios. Without the project, the deteriorated condition of the roads would limit vehicle speeds, leading to higher fuel consumption (at 0.09 liter per vehicle-km) compared to the ‘with-project’ scenario. The project’s improved road condition leads to more efficient travel speeds, and hence lower fuel consumption (at 0.07 liter per vehicle-km). Gross GHG emission in the ‘with project’ scenario is 4,617,209 tCO2e3. Total net GHG emission is estimated to be −852,100tCO2e — a net reduction over the evaluation period (20 years). The annual average net GHG emission is −53,011tCO2e per year. The social benefit from GHG reduction is estimated to be US$60 million, based on social cost of emission reduction from the World Bank’s Guidance Note on Shadow Price of Carbon in Economic Analysis (2024). 9.

BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS Borrower’s Comments LRSP2 has been a priority project for the Government of the Lao PDR. The project supported a critical period of transition for the road sector from reactive, emergency-driven maintenance practices toward a systematic, data-informed, and climate-resilient approach to road asset management. The investments made under LRSP2 have directly strengthened the capacity of MPWT and its provincial departments (DPWTs) to plan, finance, and deliver road maintenance more effectively and sustainably.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: MPWT is particularly pleased with the institutionalization of the three-year rolling climate-resilient road maintenance planning process, which is now embedded in the government's annual budget preparation cycle. This reform represents a fundamental shift in how the Ministry approaches road asset management and reflects a long-term commitment to ensuring that Lao PDR's road network can withstand the growing impacts of climate change. The use of risk-informed planning tools, including the Integrated Road Asset Management System (IRAMS-2), the Road Management System (RMS), and the Provincial Road Maintenance Management System (PRoMMS) has given MPWT the institutional foundation to prioritize investments based on evidence rather than on an ad-hoc basis. The project's introduction of OPBRC on National Road 13 South contributes to the landmark achievement for the road sector in Lao PDR. NR13 South is a critical national corridor, and the OPBRC model has demonstrated that private sector pre-financing can be effectively mobilized to deliver climate-resilient rehabilitation and long-term maintenance under a single integrated contract. This modality reduces the immediate fiscal burden on government while aligning the contractor's incentives with road condition outcomes rather than volume of inputs.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Based on the success of this pilot on NR13 South under LRSP2, MPWT is committed to expanding the OPBRC approach to other priority national roads, including the ongoing NR13 North project and future operations. MPWT extends its sincere gratitude to the World Bank, the principal financier, and to the Nordic Development Fund (NDF) for their co-financing and parallel financing contributions. The Ministry acknowledges the active and consistent support provided by both partners throughout all phases of project preparation and implementation. This included technical assistance in procurement, design, and supervision; support to the development of performance-based contracting methodologies and standard bidding documents; guidance on climate resilience mainstreaming; training for MPWT and DPWT staff in PBC and OPBRC implementation, road safety audits, and environmental and social (E&S) safeguards; and close monitoring of contract implementation and safeguard compliance. This engagement was essential to the project's success and has left lasting benefits in the form of enhanced institutional capacity across the sector. MPWT also recognizes the important contribution of the NDF to the climate resilience dimensions of the project, particularly in financing climate-resilient periodic maintenance and spot improvements and the establishment of vulnerability mapping and risk-based planning tools under the RAMS/PRoMMS system.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: This support was instrumental in shifting the Ministry's planning culture from reactive emergency response to predictive, risk-informed asset management a transformation that will generate lasting dividends for the reliability and resilience of the national road network. MPWT also wishes to express its appreciation to the EIB and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) for their Page 33 Official Use Only The World Bank Lao Road Sector Project 2 (LRSP2) (P158504) ICR DOCUMENT parallel financing of sections of National Road 13 South. The participation of EIB and AIIB provided the additional scale necessary to address the full length of this critical corridor under a harmonized, performance-based contracting framework. Their adoption of the World Bank's OPBRC standards and common technical specifications ensured consistency in quality and climate resilience requirements across all sections of NR13 South, regardless of the financing source. This coordinated multi-financier approach set a strong precedent for development partner collaboration in Lao PDR's road sector, and MPWT looks forward to continued engagement with EIB and AIIB in future infrastructure initiatives.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: The Ministry acknowledges that challenges were encountered during implementation, including macroeconomic pressures, particularly the sharp depreciation of the Lao Kip and inflationary trends, which reduced the real value of Road Fund counterpart financing and constrained the scope of routine maintenance deliverable under Component 1. The Ministry is committed to addressing these fiscal challenges going forward by strengthening RMF revenues, exploring supplementary financing mechanisms including potential tolling on key corridors, and continuing to advocate for adequate budget allocations for road maintenance within the national budget framework. The integration of road asset management priorities into the draft Transport Sector Five-Year Plan (2026–2030) reflects the government's commitment to sustaining and building upon the reforms introduced under LRSP2. MPWT also recognizes the progress made on road safety under LRSP2, including the approval by the Prime Minister's Office of the National Road Safety Strategy and Action Plan (2021–2030) and Action Plan (2021–2025). The Ministry will continue to pursue the implementation of this strategy and calls on development partners to sustain their engagement on road safety as a critical cross-cutting priority for the sector. Finally, MPWT wishes to acknowledge the dedication of the Project Management Unit (PMU) and all DoR and DPWT staff who contributed to the implementation of LRSP2.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: Their efforts, alongside those of the World Bank and NDF teams, have delivered results well above original targets on direct beneficiaries, the rural population with access to an all-season road, and share of women in project-related paid employment. These results reflect the project's contribution not only to road connectivity but also to the broader development and inclusion goals of the government. Page 34 Official Use Only
